title: Osage Memory of the Ohio Valley
summary: Osage Nation oral tradition traces the Osage and other Dhegiha Siouan peoples to an ancestral homeland in the Ohio Valley.
bodyMarkdown:
The Osage call themselves Wazhazhe. One of their old names is Ni-U-Kon-Ska, "Children of the Middle Waters." Osage Nation oral tradition holds that the Osage and the other Dhegiha Siouan peoples, the Omaha, Ponca, Kaw, and Quapaw, once lived together in the Ohio Valley.

The tradition says the peoples moved west and down the Ohio long ago, then split apart. The Quapaw went down the Mississippi, a name often read as "downstream people." The Omaha, Ponca, Kaw, and Osage went up the Missouri and its branches. The [Dhegihan languages](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dhegihan_languages) these nations speak are close kin, which fits a shared past.

The Osage Nation Historic Preservation Office also points to research in languages that places early Siouan speakers in the Ohio Valley. Some scholars tie the move to the end of the Mississippian or Fort Ancient world in the 1400s and 1500s.

Historians and archaeologists still debate how much of that can be proved. No source places an Osage town at a specific site or date in Kentucky. Archaeologists have not matched any Kentucky site to the Osage by name.

The first time the Osage appear on paper is on French maps of 1673, on the Osage River in what is now Missouri. By the 1700s they were one of the strongest nations on the prairie edge, trading with the French and controlling much of present Missouri, Arkansas, Kansas, and Oklahoma.

American expansion pushed them out. Treaties in 1808 and 1825 took most of their Missouri land. The Osage moved to Kansas and then, in the 1870s, bought a reservation in what became Oklahoma. Oil found there later made the nation wealthy for a time, and led to the murders of the 1920s known as the Osage Reign of Terror.

The story of the [Quapaw, the downstream people](/stories/quapaw-the-downstream-people-of-the-ohio-valley/), follows another branch of the same family.

## Kentucky today

There is no Osage site to visit in Kentucky. The [Osage Nation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Osage_Nation) is based in Pawhuska, Oklahoma, where its museum tells the nation's own story, including its memory of the Middle Waters.
Source: [Osage Cultural History (Osage Nation Historic Preservation Office)](https://osagenation-nsn.gov/who-we-are/historic-preservation/osage-cultural-history)
Source: [Osage (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Oklahoma Historical Society)](https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=OS001)
